docs.title: Learn Ervisio Logs
docs.intro: Practical guides for collecting, finding and retaining your logs. All articles are included in the app and available to every signed-in user.
docs.copyFailed: Could not copy. Select and copy the example manually.

articles.title: Getting started
articles.summary: Create a workspace and project, send your first event, and find it in the explorer.

sections.title: Organise your logs
paragraphs: A workspace groups members and projects. Each project has its own API tokens, streams and environments. A stream groups related events, such as inventory or moderation; an environment distinguishes production from development.

sections.title: Send the first event
steps: Open the workspace tile at the top of the rail to choose a workspace. Create a project from the project list.
Open the project. The first-event guide creates an ingest token and gives you a curl request. Copy the token before leaving the page.
Send an event, then open Log Explorer. For an existing project, create tokens under Project settings → Tokens.

sections.title: Navigate
paragraphs: The rail switches workspaces and projects. The project menu opens logs, alerts, dashboards and usage. Use the project gear for project settings and Manage for workspace settings or instance administration.
Open Account for password, sessions, optional security methods, language and theme. Ctrl K (⌘K on Mac) searches navigation commands. Documentation stays available without a workspace or project.

articles.title: Send logs with the API
articles.summary: Authenticate with a project token and send JSON events from your server.

sections.title: Authentication and a single event
paragraphs: Create a project token with logs:ingest under Settings → API tokens. Replace the example URL and placeholder token with your own. The token determines the project: do not send a token from another project.
POST /api/v1/ingest accepts one JSON event. A 202 response means it was accepted into the ingestion path; search visibility can follow asynchronously.
sections.code:
curl -X POST https://logs.example.com/api/v1/ingest \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <PROJECT_INGEST_TOKEN>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"level":"INFO","event":"server.start","message":"Hello from my server","service":"my-app","attributes":{"player_id":42,"action":"join"}}'

sections.title: Batch events
paragraphs: POST /api/v1/ingest/batch takes an object with an events array. Keep a batch at or below 1000 events and the request body within 1 MiB. Check accepted and rejected in the response instead of assuming that every event was accepted.

sections.title: Event fields and retries
paragraphs: Use level, event, message and attributes to describe an event. Add stream, environment, service, host or resource for context. Use UTC RFC 3339 timestamps and keep an event id stable when retrying the same event. A 202 response follows a durable write to the spool; search visibility follows the ClickHouse write.

On 429 or 503, honour Retry-After and back off. Correct invalid events on 422, split oversized payloads on 413, and check credentials and scopes on 401/403. Inspect accepted and rejected counts in batch responses.

sections.title: API reference and OpenTelemetry
paragraphs: The versioned contract lives in api/openapi.yaml. Send OTLP/HTTP JSON or protobuf to POST /v1/logs with an ingest token. Exporters that append /v1/logs need the instance base URL.

scripts/collector-test.py prepares an isolated app, databases and a real OpenTelemetry Collector to check forwarding and search. This fixture has not run in the 0.2 validation session because the Docker daemon did not respond.

sections.title: Tags, actor and target
paragraphs: Add up to 20 tags, each 1–40 characters. Use lowercase letters, digits, dot, underscore, colon, slash or dash. Search a tag with tag:economy. Start each tag with a lowercase letter or digit.

Put actor and target inside attributes when sending JSON. Each entity has type and id; name is optional. The TypeScript SDK also accepts actor and target in event options and writes them under attributes. Keep identifiers and player names within your privacy policy.

articles.title: Search and live logs
articles.summary: Filter events, inspect their attributes, and follow incoming logs.

sections.title: Search syntax
paragraphs: Free text searches messages. Attribute filters support =, !=, ~ (contains), >, >=, <, <= and has:key. Quote values containing spaces. Use the filter builder to choose a field, operator and value.
sections.code:
tag:economy amount>=250
actor.id=17 target.type=player
reason="card declined" payment

sections.title: Read events and narrow the range
paragraphs: Rows show relative time, severity, the catalog title and a readable message. Actor, target and tag chips add context. Open a row for Who, What, Where, When and Technical groups; expand the original payload when you need JSON. Click a value or tag to add a filter.

Choose levels, event, category, stream and environment in Filters. Drag across histogram buckets to set the search range; keyboard users can select a bucket. Level chips retain their counts when you select another level. Saved views preserve your search and filters.
The Archive badge marks rows read from the archive. A partial result means part of the selected storage was unavailable; check its destination before concluding that an event is missing.

sections.title: Live and export
paragraphs: Turn on Live in the explorer to follow new events with the active text, tag, event and attribute filters. Use the time range for historical searches. A disconnected Live connection does not prove ingestion has stopped.
Export requires logs:export. Narrow the time range and filters before exporting a large result.

articles.title: Tokens and access
articles.summary: Choose the right token scopes and understand workspace roles.

sections.title: Project API tokens
paragraphs: Tokens are tied to a project. logs:ingest sends events, logs:read queries them, and logs:export permits exports. A token cannot exceed its creator’s permissions.

Create separate tokens for each service, give each only the scopes it needs, and set an expiry when appropriate. The full secret appears only once; copy it into your server’s secret configuration. Revoke a lost or exposed token and create a replacement.
Keep tokens on the server. Do not place them in browser code, client scripts, public repositories or log messages.

sections.title: Workspace roles and invitations
paragraphs: Owner manages the workspace and its owners. Admin manages projects, members, tokens and alerts. Developer manages projects, tokens and alerts and reads/exports logs. Analyst reads and exports; Viewer reads. The workspace must retain an owner.

Open Workspace settings → Members to add an existing account or invite an email address. With SMTP configured, the app sends the link; otherwise copy the returned invitation URL. The recipient must use the invited email address.
Instance administrators manage users and service configuration. Their instance role grants no workspace membership or access to tenant logs.

sections.title: Operator tokens and archive administration
paragraphs: In Administration → Operator tokens, create an evl_adm_ token with the required admin:* scopes and an expiry within one year. Copy its plaintext value once, store it as a secret and revoke it when access ends. These tokens manage the instance and tenancy; they do not read, export or delete logs.
Administration → Archive holds shared destinations and the instance cache budget. Workspace and project retention live in their scoped settings.

articles.title: Storage and retention
articles.summary: Configure S3, SFTP or a local folder and control local disk use.

sections.title: Hot data, archive and cache
paragraphs: Hot data supports recent searches; archive segments preserve older events in the selected destination. The archive cache holds local copies used for queries. Local disk usage includes hot data and that cache.

Days on local disk controls when eligible hot data can leave the local tier after safe archival. Days before deletion is the full retention period. The local cache cap is a budget, not extra retention, and is not an instantaneous hard limit for all disk usage.

sections.title: Add and activate a destination
steps: As an instance administrator, open Administration → Archive.
Add an S3 bucket, SFTP destination or absolute folder path on the server. For a folder, the service must have the required filesystem access.
Enter credentials in the form, load a file from your computer, or reference a credential file already in the configured secrets directory.
Test the destination, then activate it. Activation directs new archive segments to it; it does not migrate old segments.
Set the instance retention and cache budget. Apply a project override only where a project needs a different retention period.

sections.title: S3 fields
paragraphs: Bucket is the existing bucket name, not its URL. Region and endpoint come from the storage provider. For S3-compatible services, enter the provider’s HTTPS endpoint and enable path-style only when that service requires it. Prefix is an optional folder-like key prefix, such as ervisio-logs/.

Access key and secret key are object-storage credentials authorised for that bucket; they are not your console login or bucket name. The file picker accepts JSON with access_key and secret_key. The app saves credentials in its secrets folder and does not show their contents again.
Use the destination test to verify access. A credential that can write but cannot read or delete can still break archive queries or retention cleanup.

sections.title: SFTP and Hetzner Storage Box
paragraphs: Choose SFTP for an SSH-accessible Storage Box. Enter its host, SSH port, user and base directory, then choose password or private-key authentication. Use the SSH port supported and enabled by your provider; it is independent of the SMB port.
Pin the server host key from a trusted source. The host key identifies the storage server; it is different from your login private key. The app service needs access to the configured credentials.

sections.title: Retention and old destinations
paragraphs: Retention inherits from instance to workspace, project and stream. Set workspace and project overrides in their settings; leave a field blank to inherit it, or clear both to remove the override. Full retention expiry deletes data.

Keep old destinations reachable while catalogued segments still reference them. Switching the active destination is not a data migration. If the archiver is disabled, configure it on the server before expecting cache eviction or remote archives to work.

articles.title: FiveM integration
articles.summary: Install the server resource and forward events from ESX, ox_inventory or your own scripts.

sections.title: Install the resource
paragraphs: Download integrations/fivem/ervisio_logs from the ErvisioLogs repository into your server resources. Create a project API token with only logs:ingest, then place these convars before ensure ervisio_logs in server.cfg.
Use set for the token, never setr (replicated to clients) or sets (published in server info). Start this resource before any resource that calls its exports.
sections.code:
set ervisio_logs_url "https://logs.example.com"
set ervisio_logs_token "<PROJECT_INGEST_TOKEN>"
set ervisio_logs_environment "production"
ensure ervisio_logs

sections.title: Send an event from a server script
paragraphs: Log(stream, level, event, message, attributes) queues an event. LogBatch(events) queues multiple events. A nil stream uses the prefix mapping in config.lua, then the default stream.

The examples folder includes ESX, ox_inventory and moderation adapters. They are examples to adapt, not automatically loaded integrations. Verify their hooks and payloads against the resources on your server.

sections.title: Queue and diagnostics
paragraphs: Events are batched with retries. The queue is in memory: queued events can be lost when the server stops or crashes. Player identifiers are opt-in and sensitive attribute keys are redacted by default.
Run ervisio_logs_status in the server console to inspect queue counters. A 401/403 stops sending: fix the token and use ervisio_logs_resume.
The integration and example adapters have not been verified in game. Test them on your development server before using them in production.

sections.title: Log v2 and privacy
paragraphs: Pass a tags array as the sixth Log argument, or use tags in LogBatch events. Put actor and target entities under attributes. Project settings can create unknown streams on ingest; disable this or set a stream limit when you need a fixed catalog.

Apply the FiveM preset under Project settings → Events and fields for event titles and templates. Player names and identifiers remain opt-in in config.lua; a catalog template does not enable their collection. Test resource hooks and payloads on your game server before deployment.

articles.title: Alerts and webhooks
articles.summary: Notify a Discord, Slack or custom webhook when matching events exceed a threshold.

sections.title: Create a notification channel
paragraphs: Open Workspace settings → Notification channels. Choose a webhook, email or Telegram. Webhooks support Discord, Slack or signed JSON. For email, enter the recipient and ask an instance administrator to configure SMTP. For Telegram, enter a bot token and chat ID; the bot needs access to that chat.

Test the channel, then inspect delivery history for success or errors. The server keeps Telegram credentials encrypted and does not return the bot token. Signed JSON channels show a signing secret once; configure that secret in your receiver.

sections.title: Create an alert
steps: Open Alerts in your project and choose a template or define the search. Select event, stream, environment and levels.
Set the observation window, threshold and check interval. The rule fires when the count exceeds the threshold.
Select channels and save. Review the sentence summary and alert history. Without a channel, the rule changes state in the app without sending a notification.

sections.title: Delivery problems
paragraphs: Check whether the channel is enabled, its test succeeds, and the remote service accepts the webhook. If the rule is in an error state, inspect its history before changing the threshold.

sections.title: System alerts
paragraphs: Instance administrators configure system alerts for spool pressure, archive delay and destination failures under Administration → System alerts. These rules monitor the service; project event rules remain in the project.

articles.title: Install and update
articles.summary: Run the app through the Ervisio plugin, Docker Compose or a standalone service.

sections.title: Ervisio plugin
paragraphs: The plugin has Overview, Instance, Workspaces, Projects, Users, Archive, Server, Address and Console sections. Instance edits runtime settings; Server edits host environment values and offers an explicit restart. Console retains the last 20 operations for the current page session.

Local management uses the admin Unix socket through approved SDK capabilities. The default rootful Docker stack uses /var/lib/docker/volumes/ervisiologs_admin/_data/admin.sock; standalone uses /run/ervisio-logs/admin.sock. Reaching this socket grants operator management access.

For a remote instance or a custom socket location, choose HTTPS and an evl_adm_ token in Instance. Ervisio asks an administrator to approve the host and reloads the plugin on first approval; reconnect afterwards. The plugin keeps the token in page memory and omits browser cookies.

Update the plugin package in Ervisio, then update the app from its page. The package contains the matching app bundle; changing the plugin package alone does not restart or upgrade the app. The 0.2 host integration has not been verified in a real Ervisio panel.

sections.title: Docker and standalone
paragraphs: Docker installs use the release’s Compose bundle. Standalone installs use the release archive for the server architecture and its install.sh, with PostgreSQL and ClickHouse configured separately. The repository’s docs/deploy directory has the full operator instructions.
Use HTTPS for the public URL. Production mode also requires a PostgreSQL connection using TLS. Configure a trusted reverse proxy deliberately; do not publish internal database ports.

sections.title: First sign-in and recovery
paragraphs: The app’s first administrator uses the setup code configured on the server or printed in its startup logs. Ervisio does not pass its own logged-in identity to the app.
Removing the plugin does not stop or uninstall the app. App uninstall keeps the databases and retained data. Back up databases and required configuration before operational changes.

articles.title: Troubleshooting
articles.summary: Diagnose missing events, permissions, archive errors and unavailable services.

sections.title: Events do not appear
steps: Confirm the sending URL and the project that owns the token. Inspect the ingest HTTP status and any rejected events.
Clear search text and filters, choose the correct environment and stream, and widen the time range. Check the sender’s clock and event timestamps.
If accepted events stay missing, check Administration → Overview, spool backlog, service logs and database connectivity.
For FiveM, inspect ervisio_logs_status; after fixing a rejected token, run ervisio_logs_resume.

sections.title: HTTP errors
paragraphs: 401: the credential is missing, invalid, expired or revoked. 403: the credential lacks the required scope or workspace access. 413: reduce the payload. 422: correct the rejected event fields. 429/503: back off and honour Retry-After.
A 202 batch response can still contain rejected events. Read the counters and errors returned in the body.

sections.title: Storage and access problems
paragraphs: Archive destinations require the separate instance-administrator role. For credential writes, check the configured secrets directory and service permissions.

For S3, verify bucket, region, endpoint and key permissions. For SFTP, verify port, host key, authentication and directory permissions. Test the destination and keep providers holding old segments accessible.
Check Administration → Overview and backend logs for dependency failures. Remove tokens, passwords and private keys from any diagnostic text you share.

articles.title: Settings and event catalog
articles.summary: Find each setting at its instance, workspace or project scope.

sections.title: Scopes and inheritance
paragraphs: Use Administration for shared archive destinations, access, email, ingest limits and service settings. Workspace settings hold members, invitations, channels and workspace defaults. Project settings hold environments, streams, tokens, catalog and project overrides.

Each runtime setting shows its source. An environment value locks that setting; change it on the host and restart the service. A database value takes effect through the runtime settings service. Reset an override to inherit the parent value.

sections.title: Event titles and field rules
paragraphs: Open Project settings → Events and fields. Assign a title, message template, icon, category, color and up to ten featured attribute fields to each technical event name. Seen event names enter the catalog for you to describe; the FiveM preset provides editable starting values.

Templates use attribute paths such as {actor.name} and {amount}. Field rules set labels, display formats and visibility. Hiding a field changes presentation. Enable Redact to replace that field on new events before durable ingest; changing a rule does not rewrite stored events.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Choose Light, Dark or AMOLED in Account. AMOLED keeps the event area black. The interface respects the device’s reduced-motion preference for background animation.

articles.title: Account security
articles.summary: Manage password, sessions, optional authenticator codes and passkeys.

sections.title: Password and sessions
paragraphs: Use Account to change your password or revoke another active session. A password change closes the other sessions. If you forgot the password, request a reset link from sign-in; the instance needs working SMTP to send it.

sections.title: Optional authenticator and recovery codes
paragraphs: Authenticator codes (TOTP) and passkeys are optional for each account. To enable TOTP, open Account → Security, confirm your password, add the displayed secret to an authenticator and enter its current code. For an account without a local password, sign in again through your external provider before changing security methods.

Copy the recovery codes when you enable TOTP and store them outside this account. Each code works once. Use an authenticator code or an unused recovery code when sign-in asks for verification. Disabling TOTP requires verification and removes its recovery codes.

sections.title: Passkeys
paragraphs: Use HTTPS and a browser with WebAuthn support. In Account → Security, name and add a passkey, then complete the browser’s device verification. Use the passkey button at sign-in to authenticate with that device or its synced credential.
Keep a working sign-in method before deleting a passkey. The 0.2 checks include a virtual authenticator; physical-device and real-provider sign-in still require host testing.

articles.title: Dashboards and usage
articles.summary: Build panels from saved searches and inspect project activity and quotas.

sections.title: Saved-query panels
steps: Save a search in Log Explorer with the filters and time range you want to reuse.
Open Dashboards in the project and create a panel. Select the saved query and choose count, time series or top values. Top values also needs an attribute field.
Name the panel and save. Edit or delete it from its card. Workspace permissions control panel changes and access to the underlying logs.

sections.title: Usage and quotas
paragraphs: Usage shows event counts and bytes by time and stream for the selected project. Byte totals measure uncompressed text payload, so they differ from compressed ClickHouse, archive or disk usage. Check partial-result notices before using totals.

Administrators can set ingest rate limits and daily event/byte quotas at workspace or project scope. A zero limit means unlimited. Quota counters belong to the running process and restart with it; multiple replicas do not share these counters.
